1:
Who opens the graves is disputed. Charles Ellicott says there is no break in the discourse, so the time must be the destruction of the city by the Chaldeans. John Gill allows either the Chaldeans or the Romans, and observes that it is certain the city was ploughed up by the Romans, when the graves were very likely dug open. On the motive they agree: greed, in expectation of treasure hidden in royal tombs, or sheer spite. Matthew Henry adds that the Chaldeans who could not reach the sepulchres of princes would rather play at small game than sit out, and dragged up the bones of ordinary citizens. Adam Clarke calls the practice the highest expression of hatred and contempt, and quotes a Latin poet on barbarian conquerors scattering the hallowed ashes of a city founder. Ellicott adds a later instance from the history of the Jews, when a ruler broke open the sepulchre of David to the scandal of the nation.

Henry raises a question none of the others asks: whether the prophets and priests named were the false ones, God putting this mark of ignominy on them, or the true, in which case the outrage is what the Psalmist complains of. He hopes aloud that the bones of Josiah were spared, since he had protected the bones of the man of God when he burned those of the idolatrous priests. John Calvin works the same ground more coldly. The faithful lose nothing when burial is denied them, yet do not despise it, since it is a badge of the resurrection; and God may involve his own in a disgrace which is punishment to the wicked and blessing to them. What the threat proves is that the city would be rooted up from its foundations, for kings had supposed that once hidden in their graves their bodies were sacred, and while a city stands its graves are spared. John Wesley says it in a line: not the walls only, but the very sepulchres turned up.

On the sun and moon and stars the voices turn the idolatry back on itself. Gill notes the irony, that deities which could not keep their worshippers from being dug up could not have them buried again either. Ellicott hears in the piled-up verbs an order running from the first inward impulse that prompts idolatry to its full development in ritual: the host of heaven shall look down not on crowds of worshippers but on the carcases of those whose worship brought this on them. Calvin makes the stars witnesses who approve the sentence, since nothing is more detestable to a creature than to have the glory of its Maker ascribed to it; he grants they have neither sense nor reason, and attributes reason to them only to shake the people out of their stupidity. He hears the language of adultery in the verse too, a harlot led out in disgrace before the men she sinned with, and remarks that no fornicator burns after a woman more furiously than idolaters do. On one verb he is short: some render it consulted, which he calls strained and far-fetched, though the sense comes to the same.

The last verse carries a textual choice. Gill reports that the Greek version and those that follow it make the clause a reason for what precedes, the bones being exposed because the people had chosen death rather than life; but he prefers the other sense, that the survivors will choose death. Calvin is blunter: those who take the words otherwise seem not to have understood the design, the point being that the living are worse off than the dead, and exile not one death but ten. Ellicott catches the reiteration again, a remnant of a remnant, and says that though the evil family means the whole house of Israel, the words look particularly to the exile of Judah and Benjamin.
4:
The two questions of the fourth verse are read as an appeal to ordinary sense. Matthew Henry reasons: a man who falls is not such a fool as to lie still, and the most careful traveller may miss his way, but as soon as he knows it he turns back; no man in his wits keeps a road he knows will never bring him home. Charles Ellicott would render both clauses indefinitely, shall men fall and not arise, shall one turn away and not return, and finds in them the assertion that repentance is possible in almost any case. Adam Clarke makes the halves answer each other: sinners may return to God as readily as God returns to them. John Calvin canvasses the alternatives before choosing. Most interpreters, he says, confine the verse to the Jews; of the second clause some make it, if Israel returns will not God also return, others, if Israel turns away will not God turn away too. He takes the whole as a general maxim about men, and adds that the call to repent was issued not from hope of it but to leave the perverse less excusable and to comfort the few godly who remained.

The reiterated word of the next verse Ellicott says the English loses: why does this people turn away with a perpetual turning. John Gill reports a different construction from a learned hand, making the city the subject: why does Jerusalem turn this people away with an obstinate aversion, or rather why does a stubborn aversion turn them away, addressing the magistrates. On the deceit they hold fast, three differ. John Wesley makes it the false prophets who encouraged them. Henry makes it sin itself, a great cheat they love and stick to, with the excuses and hopes of impunity that go with it. Calvin narrows it to hypocrisy, not deceiving a neighbour but the self-blinding by which men become unwilling to attend to the word.

Who says I hearkened and heard is disputed three ways. Gill reports the prophet as speaker on the authority of Kimchi and Abarbinel, and the Lord on that of the Targum. Ellicott makes it God, listening for penitence and hearing only the words of evildoers. Calvin allows that God may be meant but thinks the prophet more suitable, set as in a watch-tower, so that when they objected that he reproved them without knowing their hearts he could answer that he had looked and found nothing right. What the verse requires, Calvin says, is that a man summon himself before the tribunal of God; the question what have I done implies not merely shame but terror, and a formal owning of sins is useless. On the horse rushing into the battle Ellicott notes that the verb is properly used of a torrent in flood.

The birds are handled by naturalists as much as divines. Gill reports from the old writers that the stork leaves at the approach of winter and returns when it is over, that the temperature of the air and the instinct to breed are thought to move them, and that they travel by night; it is wonderful, he says, that they know both season and course. Ellicott dates its arrival in Palestine to March, and notes that its Hebrew name means the pious bird from its care of its young. Calvin, who says the versions differ widely over which birds are meant, answers a doubt of his own: it is nothing strange that birds high in the air should see further, but the point is that creatures never still still know their time, while a people that sits quietly at home knows nothing. Clarke puts the contrast in a line: they obey the dictates of nature and this people will not obey the law; Ellicott would render the last word ordinance, the rule of life the brutes keep and man transgresses.
8:
Who is being told that his wisdom is empty divides the voices. Charles Ellicott puts the question to the priests and prophets as the recognised expounders of the Law, but not to them alone, since the order of scribes was already rising into notice; the man to whom the recovered book of the Law was handed belonged to it, and that discovery would have given their work fresh impetus. John Wesley addresses it to the whole body of the people, allowing that the mention of the Law may glance particularly at the priests. John Calvin notes that interpreters generally confine it to the priests, the false prophets and the chiefs, because those men arrogated the knowledge of the Law, and argues instead that it belongs to the whole nation, since all of them from the least to the greatest reckoned themselves wise enough. He makes the point from his own day, where nobody can bear to be admonished and the rudest man will answer, do you take me for a child, or, as the saying goes, for a goose; and he supposes the Jews met the prophet the same way, asking whether he treated them as barbarians who had never been taught how to live.

The clause about the pen is read three different ways. Adam Clarke takes it of the text itself, calling it the deceitful pen of the scribes and holding that they wrote falsely with the truth before them. Ellicott renders the whole verse otherwise, that the lying pen of the scribes has made the Law into a lie, and explains it not of corrupting a text but of emptying it of its noblest meaning by sophistry; he notes that the pen meant is the iron stylus for engraving on stone, and remarks that in protesting against the casuistry of the scribes Jeremiah anticipates a later teacher. Calvin takes the vanity to be practical rather than textual. If they had truly had the Law, the charge of double folly could not have been brought; but since their whole life proclaimed them insane, the writing of it was so far wasted on them, and the teachers laboured for nothing. John Gill keeps it simplest, that they boasted continually of being wise while they were more stupid than the birds just named.

Who the wise men of the ninth verse are is disputed in its turn. Ellicott distinguishes them from the scribes as students of the ethical books rather than of the Law, and recalls that an earlier reign had been memorable for such studies; they too kept within traditional maxims and perhaps laid more stress on ceremonial than on moral obligation, so that when the word came straight from the lips of prophets they would not hear it. Calvin thinks it better to refer the wise men here to the people at large and to keep the shame named later in the chapter for the teachers who promised peace where there was no peace.

That they are ashamed Calvin will not read as a present fact, since he has already said more than once that this people were too hardened to blush. He takes it as a punishment still to come: they have an iron front now and think they can elude God and his servants, but he will take them unawares and shake off the masks they hide behind. The third verb he explains as the work of a fowler, God laying snares for men who trust their own subterfuges and keep devising new schemes to slip past him; and he closes with an old proverb, that he hates the wise man who is not wise for himself. Gill puts the same thing without the machinery, that they will be ashamed of the very wisdom they boasted of when it turns out to be folly and of no profit to them.
10:
All four voices notice at once that this passage is not new. Adam Clarke says flatly that from here to the fifteenth verse the words are repeated from the sixth chapter. Keil and Delitzsch call it a warning reiterated from a former discourse, strengthened here by the threat that God will sweep them utterly away because the nation has become an unfruitful vine and fig tree. John Calvin agrees and defends it: what has been forgotten, or never touched the heart in the first place, must be said again to the deaf and the slothful. John Gill handles the verse chiefly by cross-reference, adding only that the wives are given to strangers, than which nothing could be a sorer temporal punishment.

Calvin takes the two halves of the threat as the two worst things that happen to a conquered people. Of the first he says that nothing is more distressing than to have a wife snatched away, and that husbands offered the choice would prefer instant death to bearing such a disgrace. Of the second he fastens on the word for those who take the fields, which he renders inheritors, and argues that the word settles the length of the calamity: enemies often plunder everything and yet keep no long hold of the land, whereas inheritors possess by a kind of hereditary right. So their confidence was absurd, since they supposed the land so given them that it could never be taken away, when God would never have expelled them had they not defiled it. He adds that the particle at the head of the verse is used by anticipation and would read better as a because, and sets out his own version accordingly. On the covetousness that follows, one kind of sin is put for all, gathering under it every fraud and injustice by which men harassed one another.

At the healing of the hurt Calvin narrows the charge from the whole people to the priests and prophets. It is an inexcusable crime, he says, in men appointed to lead others to be no better than the common sort, since they corrupt the community twice over, by example and by teaching. He calls them foolish physicians laying plasters over the wrath of God, and takes the doubling of the word peace as a measure of their security, since they deceived the people not once but went on obstinately. The closing clause may be read two ways, either that God exposed their madness by the event, or that they promised peace while there was plainly no prosperity to promise it from.

On the failure to blush Calvin says that when no shame remains the case is past remedy. He offers two accounts. It may mean that even when God brought their conduct home and convicted them so that no evasion was left, they felt nothing; or it may refer to the conviction of actual suffering, since they were by then nearly consumed with miseries. That they shall fall among them that fall he explains by the way men encourage one another, each taking hope of impunity from seeing his neighbours as bad as himself. He also uses the verse to sort the chapter into two parties: the wise men put to shame earlier were the people whom the priests and prophets had deluded, while those who cannot blush here are the deluders, and the sentence tells them the punishment will reach them too. He notes in passing that this verse is not quite identical with its parallel in the sixth chapter, and gives his own rendering of the difference.
13:
The opening threat turns on a play the translators cannot keep. John Gill renders it gathering I will gather them, into one place and there destroy them, citing three Jewish authorities for consumption. Charles Ellicott gives it as gathering, I will sweep away, and notes that the two verbs are all but identical in sound and spelling, so that the phrase has nearly the force of the emphatic Hebrew doubling. John Calvin says the verb properly means to collect and only by metaphor to destroy, and adds his usual qualification: the prophets speak of the nation as a body, and God always preserved a remnant.

What the empty vine and fig tree stand for divides the two fullest voices. Ellicott points out that the words there shall be are not in the Hebrew, so the verse describes not a judgment on the state of the nation but that state itself: there are no grapes, no figs, the leaf fadeth, the nation being a degenerate vine and a barren fig tree; and this teaching, he notes, is taken up again in the Gospels. Matthew Henry knows that reading, that the words intimate their sin, God finding not so much as leaves, but prefers to take them of judgments, either literally, the enemy stripping the vines, or, as he thinks better, figuratively, that they shall be left nothing to make their hearts glad. From the clause that follows he draws his rule, that the gifts of God are held on condition and are forfeited when the condition fails.

That clause is itself contested. Ellicott reports two renderings, one making it I gave them that which they transgress, meaning the law of righteousness, the other, I will appoint those that shall pass over them, meaning the invaders; he prefers the first as suiting the context. Calvin canvasses the same field and comes out the other way. Some, he says, apply it to fruit stored in granaries, so that even a well provisioned people will have it all taken away, which he thinks the natural sense; the rendering they shall pass over them he calls too strained; and the reference to precepts the Jews had made void, which Ellicott prefers, he says cannot suit the passage at all.

The cry that follows is put in the mouth of the people by everyone. Gill says it is the prophet speaking in their language, on the authority of Kimchi; Ellicott calls it brought in with startling vividness, a flight into the fortified towns that is without hope, the silence they go into being the silence of death, to which God himself has brought them; John Wesley gives it as keeping close within the walls. Calvin insists that those who take the words for the prophet’s own sentiments are greatly mistaken, and uses the speech to describe how hypocrites behave: they feel their evils and look for remedies, but stop at the nearest shelter instead of ascending to the first cause and seeking to be reconciled with God. He marks the wordplay that carries the reproof, since the people say they will be quiet in the strong cities and are answered that the Lord has made them quiet, the same verb meaning both to rest and to be silenced. On the water of gall Ellicott says poison is implied as well as bitterness, and the plant unidentified, some proposing belladonna or colocynth from its being named with grapes and others the poppy, which the narcotic drink of the Gospel narrative may support. At the last verse Gill traces the disappointed hope to the false prophets and the confidence the walls had given; Ellicott would render the second term healing, or on another etymology quietness answered by alarm; and Calvin says they might promise themselves peace a hundred times and ruin would still be at the door.
16:
Whose horses these are they settle differently. John Gill makes them the horses of Nebuchadnezzar, and notes that John Calvin would rather call them the Lord’s, as ordered and sent by him whose war it was. Calvin does argue exactly that: the pronoun might be referred to the invading nation, since Hebrew often uses a relative without an antecedent, but he thinks it likelier that the prophet points to the first mover of the war, God sending out the armies that disturb the borders. Whether the sound carried the length of the land divides them. Gill takes it that the snorting was heard at Jerusalem, a hyperbole marking the certainty of the invasion, and John Wesley agrees. Calvin knows that reading and doubts it can be got out of the words: the simpler and truer sense, he thinks, is that while Jerusalem sat at ease the frontier was already not quiet, the city being told to notice a war that has not yet reached its gates.

Adam Clarke pauses on the trembling of the land to admire it. So terrible was the united neighing of the Babylonian cavalry, he says, that the shaking of the air made the ground tremble; and he judges the image better than the celebrated line of Virgil about hoofs shaking the crumbling plain, since it is easier to shake the ground with the prancing of horses than by their neighing alone. Charles Ellicott keeps to the history, that an army whose most terrible arm was cavalry was a special terror to this people, and that the sound is heard at the northern boundary; and he pauses to dismiss a patristic reading which found in the tribe named here the coming of Antichrist, calling it one of the eccentricities of exegesis. Calvin notes an irregularity of number in the closing clause, a city put for cities, since the neighbouring towns are threatened too.

The serpents that follow are taken by everyone for the invaders. Gill makes them the Chaldeans, comparable to such creatures for the mischief they would do; Clarke calls them symbols of a foe that would rather kill than take ransom; Calvin says the point is that escape is impossible, since from many serpents at once a man can hardly get away. Ellicott works on the words. The change of figure is sudden, and may start from the fiery serpents of the wilderness or from the serpent and adder to which the same tribe was likened in the old blessing; the genus and species of the serpents of Scripture are hard to fix; the two words stand in apposition; and cockatrice cannot be right, since as an English word it belongs to legendary zoology, one version giving basilisk and another adder. Whatever the creature, it is a hissing venomous snake, and the same symbol had already been used of this power by the older prophet.

On the charming the two fullest voices take opposite ground. Ellicott treats the practice as real and long-established, noting that serpent-charming appears very early, as it still does in Egypt and India, and that the figure is that of the deaf adder which refuses the voice of the charmer and stands for an implacable enemy. Calvin raises the question directly, whether serpents can be driven off by incantation, and answers that the prophet does not vouch for the thing but speaks according to the common opinion of men, which Virgil expressed when he wrote that a snake is dissolved in the meadow by singing. What the figure is for, Calvin says, is irony at the expense of their own devices: they think to soothe their enemies with flatteries and bribes and to have means at hand for turning the danger aside, and are told that all their charms will be useless. John Wesley reduces it to a line, that there will be no appeasing that fury by any method.
18:
The first word of the passage is one of the hardest in the chapter. Charles Ellicott says the term rendered comfort occurs nowhere else and has been very differently understood, and takes the clause as a cry uttered after a pause, mourning for a comfort that is dead and gone. John Calvin sets out the whole field. The ancient versions all differ, he says, and it is hard to make the original agree with any of them; the word may be a personal noun, my consoler, meaning the man’s own soul, or a common noun, my consolation or my strength, meaning God; one scholar derives the verb from a root for laughing and renders it as a bitter grin of pain, and another divides the word in two, making a negative and a noun of healing, so that the line becomes sorrow upon me past my remedying. Calvin takes the simplest course and reads it as a common noun addressed to God.

Whose heart it is that faints they do not agree on. John Wesley says the prophet now seems to speak, and to show how greatly the calamity of the people affected him; John Gill agrees, making this the very thing that made his heart faint, such was his sympathy with his countrymen. Calvin will not have it. The verse, he thinks, sets out the perverse character of the people, who tried by sheer obstinacy to push every punishment away; and it cannot be referred to the prophet or to men like him, since the servants of God are easily terrified by his judgment, while it is the hypocrite who hardens himself.

The cry from far off is read two ways, and Calvin allows both. Interpreters, he reports, apply the phrase to the invading nations, so that the people are being told that the very distance of the Chaldeans and Assyrians is what makes them secure, and that their enemies will come nonetheless; he says he has no objection if the words are taken so, since hypocrites draw their confidence from the look of the present. The other sense he thinks equally suitable, and it is the one Ellicott adopts: the verse should read that the cry comes from the land of those that are far off, the prophet dramatising the future and hearing the exiles call from their captivity. Their question, Ellicott adds, is asked half in despair and half in complaint, and it is answered not by consolation but by a counter-question from God himself, which is why they were forsaken. Calvin notes that the prophet takes three parts in a single verse, denouncing the ruin, speaking in the person of the people, and then answering them in the name of God.

What has failed by the end of the summer divides them again. Ellicott takes it as famine: they are like men in a year when the harvest passed and there was no crop to reap, the second word being better rendered the fruit-gathering, and the whole formula having probably become proverbial for extremest misery; he adds the calendar, that the barley-harvest fell with the Passover, the wheat-harvest with Pentecost and the fruit-gathering with the autumn feast. Adam Clarke also calls it a proverb, but hears in it the two years of the siege, deliverance looked for in the first year and hoped for in the second and never coming. Calvin makes the failure diplomatic rather than agricultural. The people had counted on their allies, and he reports that some take the harvest to mean the season when the Egyptians would be free to march and provisioned for it; he prefers to make the words cover the whole campaigning season, so that the sense is that if help were coming it would have come, and nobody marches once winter shuts him in. Gill adds only the month the harvest fell in.
21:
Who says I am hurt has a reported history. John Gill notes that one expositor made the words God and one paraphrase made them the city, but follows Kimchi in giving them to the prophet; he offers a second rendering, that the breach of his people is the breaking up of the city. Charles Ellicott says the prophet speaks again in his own person, crushed in the crushing of his people, his face darkened like a mourner, and John Wesley reads the blackness as the dress of deep mourning. John Calvin agrees that the prophet now takes to himself what he had ascribed to the people, and explains why he keeps changing his manner of speech: he was at a loss for any address strong enough to get through hearts of iron, which is why the chapter runs through so many figures. He imagines the answer the prophet got, that his grief was his own business and nobody had asked his pity, the people being content with their lot and preferring he wept at home. Calvin gives the verse twice, once keeping the figure, that he was bruised and blackened and desolation took hold of him, and once stripped of it, that he sorrowed and mourned and astonishment took hold of him; that astonishment being the exact opposite of the torpor of a people who felt no fear.

What the balm is the naturalists among them argue. Gill doubts it is balsam, since balsam grew west of the Jordan near Jericho and not in the country beyond, and prefers turpentine or rosin, a gum that drops from pines and is good for healing. Calvin agrees that rosin is meant, a thick liquid that flows not from every tree but from the pine, and though the whole country produced it he thinks it named from Gilead because there it was more abundant; the word can also mean balsam, he says, and on that point every man may follow his own opinion, since the Jews do not agree. Both dismiss the rendering treacle, Gill quoting Calvin for the reason, that treacle is a compound of many ingredients while this is a single gum. Ellicott reports that naturalists identify the gums of Gilead with the terebinth or with mastic, notes that they were exported for embalming the dead, and says a plaster of such gum was the standard prescription for a wound.

How the two questions are to be answered is the last and sharpest division. Adam Clarke answers both in the affirmative and turns the verse into an indictment. Is there balm in Gilead? Yes, the most excellent in the world. Is there a physician? Yes, men well skilled to apply it. Why then no recovery? Because they never applied to him or used the balm, and men die when they will not take the remedy. He carries it into the spiritual case, concluding that it is not from any want of grace or of the means of grace that men are not saved, but because they make no use of them or a bad use; and he quotes an old manuscript version he owned, which asks whether gum is not in Gilead, or a leech not there. Ellicott reads the question the same way, a parable in which the prophets were the physicians and repentance the balm. Calvin takes it the other way. The verse means, he says, that the slaughter would be so fatal that remedies would be sought in vain and the disease was incurable; ungodly men look round on every side when danger appears and rest secure as soon as they think anything can protect them, and the prophet speaks to dispel such confidence. He adds that the whole passage from the nineteenth verse looks forward to the captivity, so the questions should stand in the past tense: was there balm in Gilead, was there a healer there.
